title: When should you cache/persist (expensive computation + multiple reuses: iterative ML, multiple downstream branches, interactive exploration) and when should you NOT (dataset used once, dataset is tiny, caching everything causes memory pressure and eviction)?
shortTitle: When to cache/persist and when not to

s1_definition.profdef: You should cache or persist a dataset when it is expensive to compute and reused multiple times, so that the one-time cost of storing it is repaid by avoiding repeated recomputation — classic cases are iterative machine learning that passes over the same data, a dataset feeding several downstream branches, and interactive exploration. You should not cache when a dataset is used only once, because there is no reuse to benefit from, when it is tiny and cheap to recompute, or when caching everything causes memory pressure that evicts useful cached data and slows the whole job.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a clerk at the National Bank of India deciding what to keep ready on his desk. He should keep the hard-won summary that ten different reports all need, because building it once and reusing it saves hours. He should not clutter his desk with a figure he will use only once, or with a trivial total he can redo in a second, or with so many papers that the desk overflows and he starts losing the important ones. Keeping things handy is valuable only when they are both costly to produce and needed again; otherwise it just wastes space.
s1_definition.oneliner: Cache when a dataset is both expensive to produce and reused several times; do not cache single-use data, trivially cheap data, or so much data that eviction and memory pressure hurt the whole job.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You should cache or persist a dataset when it is expensive to compute and reused multiple times, so that the one-time cost of storing it is repaid by avoiding repeated recomputation — classic cases are iterative machine learning that passes over the same data, a dataset feeding several downstream branches, and interactive exploration. You should not cache when a dataset is used only once, because there is no reuse to benefit from, when it is tiny and cheap to recompute, or when caching everything causes memory pressure that evicts useful cached data and slows the whole job.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a clerk at the National Bank of India deciding what to keep ready on his desk. He should keep the hard-won summary that ten different reports all need, because building it once and reusing it saves hours. He should not clutter his desk with a figure he will use only once, or with a trivial total he can redo in a second, or with so many papers that the desk overflows and he starts losing the important ones. Keeping things handy is valuable only when they are both costly to produce and needed again; otherwise it just wastes space.

**One line to remember:** Cache when a dataset is both expensive to produce and reused several times; do not cache single-use data, trivially cheap data, or so much data that eviction and memory pressure hurt the whole job.

sections.s2_technical:
The decision rests on two factors: how expensive the dataset is to compute, and how many times it is reused. Caching pays off only when both are high, because caching has a cost — it computes and stores the data on the first action and consumes executor memory thereafter. If a dataset is expensive to build and read many times, the first action pays the full cost plus storage, and every later action is nearly free, so the total work drops sharply. This is why the canonical good cases are iterative machine learning, where training loops over the same dataset dozens of times; multiple downstream branches, where one cleaned dataset feeds several reports or writes; and interactive exploration, where an analyst runs many queries against the same base.

The clearest signal that caching will help is more than one action on the same expensive lineage. Because every action re-triggers the whole lineage by default, two actions on an uncached expensive dataset means computing it twice, three means three times, and so on. Caching collapses all of those into one computation plus cheap reads. So whenever I see a dataset that is the shared input to several actions and is costly to derive, that is a cache.

Equally important is knowing when not to cache. If a dataset is used only once — computed and then written or collected a single time — caching gives no benefit because there is no second read to speed up; you just pay the storage overhead for nothing. If a dataset is tiny or trivially cheap to recompute, caching is pointless because recomputation costs almost nothing, and the cache just occupies memory. And the most damaging mistake is caching everything indiscriminately: executor memory is finite, so over-caching causes eviction, where useful cached partitions are pushed out to make room, and under the memory-only levels evicted partitions are dropped and recomputed, which can make the job slower than if nothing were cached, while also increasing garbage-collection pressure.

A senior nuance is that caching interacts with the rest of the plan. Caching a dataset before a point where its lineage branches is especially valuable because it prevents recomputing the shared prefix for each branch. Conversely, caching a dataset that is only narrowly transformed and used once adds no value. It is also good practice to unpersist a cached dataset once its reuse is finished, so it does not hold memory for the rest of a long job. The disciplined approach is to cache deliberately at the specific points where an expensive result is genuinely reused, and to measure in the Spark UI whether cached data is actually being hit and whether eviction is occurring. In the bank, I cached the shared cleaned transaction dataset that fed five reports, but I never cached single-pass extracts or tiny reference lists, and I unpersisted caches when their phase of the job ended.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A cleaned dataset feeds five reports and is expensive. This is exactly a case to cache.

Problem 2 — A one-time extract is written once and never reread. This is exactly a case not to cache.

Problem 3 — Caching everything evicts the useful cache and slows the job. This is exactly the over-caching mistake.

The mini-project models the decision in Java. A `CacheAdvisor` takes a dataset's compute cost, reuse count, size, and the remaining cache capacity, and decides whether to cache, explaining the reason. A `MemoryBudget` tracks capacity and simulates eviction when over-caching. The demo evaluates several of Rajesh's and Priya's banking datasets and shows cache, skip, and eviction outcomes.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a one-hundred-megabyte cache budget and five datasets with different cost, reuse, and size characteristics.

Step 1: The cleaned transactions dataset has a high compute cost of nine and is reused five times by five reports. It passes both rules and fits the budget, so it is cached, consuming forty megabytes.

Step 2: The daily extract is expensive at eight but used only once, so despite its cost the advisor skips it — there is no second read to benefit, so caching would only waste memory.

Step 3: The account-type lookup is reused four times but has a trivial compute cost of one, so the advisor skips it because recomputing it is practically free and caching it would needlessly occupy memory.

Step 4: The machine-learning feature matrix is very expensive at ten and reused twenty times in a training loop, the ideal caching case, and it fits in the remaining budget, so it is cached, bringing used memory to ninety megabytes.

Step 5: The branch rollup is expensive at seven and reused three times, so it is a genuine candidate, but only ten megabytes of budget remain and it needs forty. The memory budget refuses it with an eviction warning, and the advisor skips caching it here rather than evicting the more valuable cached data.

Step 6: The journey shows the rule in action — cache only expensive and reused datasets, skip single-use and trivially cheap ones, and respect the memory budget so that over-caching does not evict the data that actually matters.

2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] SKIP 'daily_extract': used once → no reuse benefit
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] SKIP 'account_type_lookup': tiny/cheap to recompute → caching wastes memory
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] CACHE 'ml_features': expensive (cost=10) AND reused 20x
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [WARNING] EVICTION: caching 'branch_rollup' (40000000B) exceeds budget — evicts useful cached data, may recompute
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] SKIP 'branch_rollup': over budget → do NOT cache here
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] cache memory used = 90000000B of 100000000B

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Dataset usage (cost, reuseCount, size)
    │
    ▼  CacheAdvisor
  reuseCount <= 1 ? ── yes ──→ SKIP (used once, no benefit)
  computeCost <= 2 ? ── yes ──→ SKIP (tiny/cheap)
  fits in budget ?  ── no  ──→ SKIP (over-cache → eviction)
    │ all pass
    ▼
  CACHE (expensive + reused + fits)

  cleaned_txns(9,5x,40MB) → CACHE     daily_extract(8,1x) → SKIP
  account_lookup(1,4x)   → SKIP       ml_features(10,20x,50MB) → CACHE
  branch_rollup(7,3x,40MB) → SKIP (no budget → would evict)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The decision to cache rests on two factors: how expensive a dataset is to compute, and how many times it is reused. Caching pays off only when both are high, because caching itself has a cost — it computes and stores the data on the first action and then occupies executor memory. When a dataset is both expensive to build and read many times, the first action pays the full cost plus storage and every later action is nearly free, so the total work drops sharply. The canonical good cases are iterative machine learning that loops over the same data many times, a cleaned dataset feeding several downstream branches like multiple reports, and interactive exploration where an analyst runs many queries against the same base. The clearest signal is more than one action on the same expensive lineage, because every action re-triggers the whole lineage by default, so caching collapses repeated recomputation into one computation plus cheap reads.

Knowing when not to cache is just as important. If a dataset is used only once, caching gives no benefit because there is no second read to speed up, so you pay storage overhead for nothing. If it is tiny or trivially cheap to recompute, caching is pointless because recomputation costs almost nothing. And the most damaging mistake is caching everything indiscriminately: executor memory is finite, so over-caching causes eviction, where useful cached partitions are pushed out, and under memory-only levels evicted partitions are dropped and recomputed, which can make the job slower than caching nothing while also raising garbage-collection pressure.

In my project at the National Bank of India I applied this deliberately. I cached the shared cleaned transaction dataset that fed five different reports, because building it once and reusing it five times was a big win, and I cached feature matrices reused across machine-learning iterations. But I never cached single-pass extracts that were written once, nor tiny reference lists that cost nothing to rebuild, and I was careful not to over-cache and evict the data that mattered. I also made a habit of calling unpersist when a cached dataset's phase of the job was finished so it did not hold memory for the rest of a long run, and I checked the Spark UI's storage tab to confirm the cache was actually being hit and that eviction was not happening.
